summary: Silent Robots is an interactive educational website that tells the story of the robots NASA left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space, such as Surveyor 3, Viking 1, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Pioneer 10, Kepler and Ingenuity. It answers the challenge by turning historical and scientific data into experiences that children choose according to how they learn: reading an illustrated book, exploring a timeline (also in 3D), watching an animated short film, answering readings and quizzes, or playing memory match, word search, crossword and puzzle games. Each machine “tells” its mission, what it discovered and how it ended. It matters because young people usually hear only about active missions; this project shows them that these explorers are still part of the history and the science that made today’s achievements possible. It is available in English and Spanish, with accessibility options.
details:
What it does and how it works. The site has three sections:

- Stories: a 7-page illustrated book, a timeline from 1967 to 2024 with a 3D view, and a 6-scene animated short film with subtitles and narration.

- Learn and practice: 8 readings with quizzes, fill-in-the-blank sentences, and a nine-question quiz with explanations.

- Games: memory match, word search, crossword and puzzle. All have three levels (easy, medium and hard). Every time the user enters, the themes, words and pieces change, and a “Shuffle” button rearranges them. In the puzzle, when the image is finished, a question appears to check what the player learned.

Benefits and accessibility. Each child can learn in their own way: reading, watching, listening or playing. The site offers light and dark mode, high contrast, adjustable text size, and read-aloud using the browser’s voice (with pause and resume in the book and the short film). English is the default language, with a selector for Spanish, and the content of the games changes depending on the language rather than just being translated.

Expected impact. To bring students and space enthusiasts closer to the history of robotic missions, spark curiosity about science, and serve as a support tool in class or at home.

Tools used. Pure HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no libraries or frameworks, with our own SVG drawings and the browser’s speech synthesis API. We also used Visual Studio Code, Inkscape, GitHub, NotebookLM, Gemini and Claude. Designed to open in common browsers and on phones, tablets or computers.

Creativity. The robots tell their own story instead of listing facts, and each game is tied to a real reading or mission. The logo and drawings are original to the team, with no NASA brand elements.

Factors considered. Accuracy of the data, taken from NASA sources (NSSDCA and science.nasa.gov), a young audience, accessibility, a variety of ways to learn, and replayability.
